In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV is not a liver disease per se, but it is a disease that can affect liver health and liver disease.
the liver pathology in HIV infection has changed significantly with the advent of antiretrovival therapy.
the liver pathology of people living with HIV has evolved with the improvement in antiretoviral therapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV and antiretoviral therapy are associated with a spectrum of liver diseases, including viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, nonalcoholic fatty disease, and liver cancer.
liver pathology in people living with HIV has shifted from opportunistic infection and immune reconstitution to metabolic liver disease.
HIV infection, antiretrovial therapy, and coinfections with hepatitis C, B, and D, as well as alcohol and metabolic diseases, are the main drivers of liver pathology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
liver pathology findings are highly dependent on the epidemiology of HIV infection, antiretrovival therapy, and the setting in which the liver biopsy is being performed.
HIV is a systemic illness, and liver disease is a significant contributor to mortality in this population.
liver pathologists should consider the clinical context of HIV disease and its therapy, as well as the geographic region, when interpreting liver pathology specimens.
